job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in a terraced house in Sheffield with my friend Tomas, and my days start with coffee and the job alerts. I spend the morning on applications and the afternoon on a small home project, a solar charge controller on a breadboard. Evenings I go to a graduate meetup or help Tomas cook. It's busy enough that I don't feel idle, but I'm still unemployed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what did the internship involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did electrical and electronic engineering at Sheffield Hallam and got a good result. I spent eight weeks at Brightfield Solar, a small installer, drawing wiring layouts and visiting roofs with a technician called Gareth. They liked me but had no graduate post. My mum is a nurse in Bradford and could lend me a bit if rent gets tight, and I have about two months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's roughly what I expected, so no big news. I'd tell friends to stop panicking, and I'd use the AI tools a bit for tidying emails and checking code snippets, same as now. Online I'd share articles on how the energy transition still needs electricians and engineers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's not the AI that worries me, it's rent. Brightfield said maybe next spring, but small firms say that to everyone. I've got two months of savings and a landlord who put rent up last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending around 25 applications a month, with a focus on solar, grid and battery firms. I'd ask Gareth to introduce me to two installers who might take a junior. I'd also keep using AI tools to polish my cover letters, because a tidy letter does help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, to be honest. It feels fine in the big picture but heavy at the kitchen table every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you worry about first if no job came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, no question. My share is 380 a month, and the council tax split on top. My mum says she'd cover a month or two, but I don't want to ask her because she's already stretched on a nurse's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should do something about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, really. Energy firms get big subsidies and then hire nobody young. I'd like a rule that firms taking green money must run a graduate scheme.

Use AI to polish cover letters each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the point where we need rules, and quickly. If AI takes coding, checking and planning, then graduates get squeezed first and nobody protects us. I'd say it to friends and I'd say it at the graduate meetup, where there are about thirty people in my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, half of my degree is design checking and calculations, and that's exactly what the card says gets automated. I'd expect smaller graduate intakes and more pressure to deliver with software. The good news is that I already use the tools, so I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a short course on power systems modelling software and an official cloud certificate, then learn to use AI for design checks. I'd aim for jobs where electricity meets hands-on work, like battery installs, since robots arrive there more slowly. I'd also join an engineers' union branch and start going to its meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, a bit tense. I like learning new things, but I don't like being made to run faster just to stay in the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join a union. Have you ever been in one before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as a member, but my mum is in one at the hospital and it's helped her through two reorganisations. My mum says you only notice a union when you need it. For graduates, I think a union could set minimum pay for entry jobs and stop firms replacing juniors with software for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the entry jobs simply aren't there at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go for a master's in energy systems, which is a path I've already looked at in Edinburgh. My mum would help with a loan, and I'd hope the market looks better when I finish. It's a gamble, but the other option is to wait with nothing.

I'd raise it at the graduate meetup, where about thirty people are in my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and that politicians are asleep. Two years isn't enough to retrain a country. I'd call for paid retraining and a tax on the firms that profit, and I'd take part in a protest if one is organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree is in trouble. If thinking work is done cheaper in two years, junior engineers like me are the first to be replaced, and the three extra years for robots would only help site workers. I'd feel I picked the wrong time to graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone and hold my savings. I'd talk to my mum about moving back to Bradford to save rent, then apply for anything with hands-on work like installing or maintaining equipment. I'd also join every group pushing for support, including the union and a graduate forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but fired up, like when a storm is coming and you start checking the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going to need a plan for rent, and let's cook big batches of food and share costs. Tomas is a computing graduate, so he's in the same boat. We'd probably end up at the graduate meetup arguing about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move back home, after living independently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, but I'd hate it. It would feel like going backwards, even though it makes sense. I think I'd do it for six months and treat it as a pause, not a defeat.

I'd call for paid retraining funded by a tax on the **firms that profit**, and join a protest.

steps.text: Move back to Bradford for six months to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and we should use it to push for laws on how companies use AI and a fair share of the profit. I'd tell friends to get into jobs near the energy grid. I'd also say that unions have to move now, not once it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm cautious but not terrified. If I get a job within a year I'd have a few years of experience, and electricity work has a hands-on side. The thinking tasks go on the stated date though, so I'd want to move toward site and field roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I can get, then spend evenings on an apprenticeship-style qualification for commissioning batteries and substations. I'd save a third of every pay cheque and pay off my loan early. I'd also vote for any party that backs graduate schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mixed with some dread. There's time, but the clock is audible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust companies to use the window well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I think they'd use it to cut costs. That's why I'd want unions and rules, so the window isn't used only by owners. It's like how the energy firms found excuses to delay solar subsidies for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the saving plan look like in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I land an entry salary I'd put about a third of it aside, the rest on rent and food. In twelve months that's a real cushion, maybe four months of living costs. I'd rather feel ready than spend on gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people if governments and employers start today. I'd push for AI rules and for training that doesn't bankrupt people. I'd tell friends that the energy sector will need people for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay. Ten years gives me time to build a career, maybe become a design engineer, and to learn both the tools and the field work. I'd still keep a backup, since thinking work goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, learn the field work, then go for a chartered engineer qualification and an AI-in-engineering short course. I'd also volunteer with a community solar group, which adds experience and good people. I'd save for a deposit on a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, but not complacent. I like the idea of a decade because it feels like a real plan, not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the community solar group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the group, Sheffield Sun Co-op, installs panels on schools and churches, and they let volunteers shadow the electricians. It gives me hands-on hours and a reason to turn up at weekends. It's also the kind of work that I'd be proud to explain to my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what's the thing that could still go wrong in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The danger is that the benefits go to a few firms, and the rest of us get told to be grateful for crumbs. If that happens my plan only protects me, not my mum or the people at the meetup. That's the part I'd keep an eye on.

I'd push for AI rules and training that doesn't bankrupt people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time and the rules wouldn't be ready. What would help is paid retraining, entry-level jobs protected by law for a few years, and rent help for graduates. My mum's support would matter too, even if I hate relying on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd feel guilty about using AI to get ahead. A little, since I know it may be the thing that replaces people like me. But I'd rather use it than be the person who refused and lost out. If I get a job, I'll use my seat to argue for sharing the gains.

headlineQuote: I'd rather use it than be the person who refused and lost out.
portrait: David is a **good-result** electrical engineering graduate sharing a rented room in Sheffield, with no offer yet.
His mother is a nurse and a union member, and that shapes his instinct to **organise** and ask for rules.
He uses AI tools now and then and learns new things once they're proven, so he plans courses rather than waiting.
Mood moves from **anxious** at the two-year case to uneasy at ten years.
He blames subsidised energy firms and weak rules, and wants graduate schemes and retraining funded fairly.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, because there'd be no time to prepare and rules wouldn't be ready.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining, **protected entry jobs** for a few years and rent help for graduates.
His mother's support, even if he dislikes relying on it.
